channel.description: Recent content in Planning on Best of AI

item.title: Basecamp
item.description:
Basecamp takes a different approach from most project tools. Each project is a self-contained workspace with sections for to-dos, a message board for announcements and discussions, a shared schedule, documents and files, and a group chat called Campfire. Instead of dozens of views and customization options, it offers a fixed, simple structure that’s easy to learn, and encourages asynchronous communication over constant meetings.

The company that makes it, 37signals, is outspoken about its philosophy: calm, focused work and fewer meetings. Features like automatic check-ins replace status meetings, Hill Charts show progress visually, and notifications are designed to be quiet by default. Clients can be invited into projects, which makes it popular with agencies and small businesses.

item.title: Morgen
item.description:
Morgen is a calendar and planner. Users connect Google, Outlook, iCloud, and other calendars to see everything in one view, and bring in tasks from tools like Notion, Todoist, and Linear. Tasks can be dragged onto the calendar to block time for them.

The planner feature suggests where tasks fit in the day, taking events, deadlines, and durations into account, and rearranges when plans change. Scheduling links let others book time, with rules for availability and buffers. Frames let users reserve time for certain types of work.

item.title: SavvyCal
item.description:
SavvyCal tries to make scheduling feel less like a chore. Instead of a one-sided grid of available times, the invitee can overlay their own calendar, which helps them see conflicts and pick a time that works for both sides. The host can also mark preferred slots, so the invitee sees which options are ideal.

Other features cover business needs. Teams can use round robin and collective scheduling, polls help find a time for groups, and links can be personalized for different meetings. Integrations connect to calendars, video tools, and CRMs, and payments can be collected for paid sessions. Branding options keep the experience consistent.

item.title: Trello
item.description: Trello organizes work on a board. Lists represent stages like To Do, Doing, and Done, and each task is a card that you drag from list to list. Cards can hold descriptions, checklists, due dates, attachments, comments, and assigned members. The simplicity is the point: most people learn it in minutes, which makes it popular for small teams, personal projects, content calendars, and simple workflows like hiring or event planning.

item.title: Wrike
item.description:
Wrike is used by teams that coordinate lots of work. Projects can be viewed as lists, boards, Gantt charts, or calendars, and tasks carry dependencies, owners, due dates, and custom fields. Request forms and approvals let outside teams submit work in a structured way, which helps marketing, creative, and operations groups manage intake.

AI features reduce routine effort. Wrike’s tools can summarize long comment threads, create tasks from text, draft project descriptions, and predict which projects are at risk of missing deadlines. Dashboards show workloads and progress across portfolios, and integrations connect to Slack, Salesforce, Microsoft 365, and Adobe tools. Proofing helps creative teams review assets.

item.title: skills
item.description:
This repository bundles the following skills:

  • grill-with-docs: Runs a planning session that builds a domain model and updates project docs.
  • triage: Moves issues through a defined state machine workflow.
  • improve-codebase-architecture: Scans a codebase and reports where its architecture could be deepened.
  • to-spec: Turns a conversation into a written specification for an issue tracker.
  • to-tickets: Breaks a plan into small, ordered tickets with dependencies noted.
  • implement: Builds a feature from a spec using test-driven development.
  • wayfinder: Plans large work as a set of linked decision tickets.
  • prototype: Builds a throwaway prototype to answer a design question.
  • diagnosing-bugs: Runs a structured loop for tracking down hard bugs.
  • research: Investigates a question against primary sources.
  • domain-modeling: Builds and refines a project’s domain model.
  • code-review: Reviews code against both coding standards and the original spec.

item.title: Productboard
item.description:
Productboard is a product management platform. Feedback from many sources flows into a central place, where it is linked to features and customers. Product managers see which problems come up most and who is asking, which grounds roadmap decisions in evidence.

AI helps process the volume of input. It groups similar requests, summarizes calls and tickets, and drafts specs and release notes. Prioritization frameworks score ideas against objectives, and roadmaps can be shared with stakeholders at different levels of detail.

item.title: Cal.com
item.description:
Cal.com is an alternative to Calendly built around openness. Users connect their calendars, define when they are free, and share a link that lets others book a slot. Event types handle one-on-one meetings, group sessions, and team round-robin assignments, and bookings sync to video tools and calendars.

Because the code is open source, companies can self-host it and customize it, or embed scheduling inside their own products with APIs and components. Workflows send reminders and follow-ups, payments can be collected at booking, and routing forms direct prospects to the right person. AI assistants can handle scheduling conversations.

item.title: Acuity Scheduling
item.description:
Acuity Scheduling lets people book time with you through a branded page that you can link to or embed on a website. It syncs with Google, Outlook, and iCloud calendars so you never get double-booked, and clients pick from available slots in their own time zone. It is used by coaches, therapists, tutors, salons, consultants, and other service providers who sell appointments or classes.

Beyond booking, it handles the admin around an appointment. Clients can fill out custom intake forms, pay deposits or full fees, buy packages and gift certificates, and use coupons. Automatic email and text reminders reduce no-shows, and clients can reschedule themselves. Group classes, multiple staff calendars, and multiple locations are supported on higher plans. Integrations connect to Zoom, Stripe, PayPal, QuickBooks, and Zapier.

item.title: Asana
item.description:
Asana helps teams keep track of who is doing what by when. Work is organized into projects and tasks, viewable as lists, boards, timelines, or calendars, with dependencies, owners, due dates, and custom fields. Goals connect daily tasks to company objectives, and portfolios give leaders an overview of many projects.

AI features reduce the overhead of managing work. They can generate project plans from a description, summarize updates and conversations, answer questions about project status, and spot risks to deadlines. Asana has also introduced AI teammates that can be assigned work and operate inside projects, with controls to keep humans in charge. Automations handle routing and reminders.

item.title: Calendly
item.description:
Calendly removes the back-and-forth of finding a meeting time. You connect your calendar, set the hours you are available and the types of meetings you offer, and share a link. Invitees choose a slot in their own time zone, and the event appears on both calendars with a video link added automatically. Buffers, meeting limits, and minimum notice settings keep the schedule manageable.

Teams use more advanced features. Round-robin scheduling spreads meetings across several people, collective events find times when everyone is free, and routing forms send prospects to the right person based on their answers. Workflows send reminders and follow-ups, payments can be collected through Stripe or PayPal, and integrations connect with Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, Salesforce, HubSpot, and Slack. Newer AI features help with note-taking and scheduling assistance.

item.title: Clockwise
item.description:
Clockwise worked inside Google Calendar and Slack to protect time for deep work. It looked at a team’s calendars, moved flexible meetings, and combined scattered gaps into longer blocks, aiming to cut the constant switching between tasks that fragments a workday. It could also find meeting times that worked for groups.

The product grew a following among engineering and product teams, and added AI scheduling features and a way to plan work around priorities. The company ended the service and the team joined Salesforce, where they work on AI agents. The product itself did not move over.

item.title: Height
item.description: Height set out to make project management less manual. It was a task and project tracker with a clean interface, and its main idea was that AI should do routine upkeep: sorting incoming requests, writing and updating subtasks, assigning work, and keeping descriptions consistent. Teams used it as a lighter alternative to Jira with more automation, and the product drew fans among startups for its design and its early AI features.

item.title: Linear
item.description: Linear is a project management tool aimed at product and engineering teams. Its pitch is that the tool should get out of your way: pages load instantly, nearly everything can be done from the keyboard, and the data model is opinionated about how software gets built. Work is tracked as issues, grouped into cycles (time-boxed sprints), projects, and initiatives, with roadmaps on top for the longer view. Many teams switch to it from Jira because there is far less configuration to maintain.

item.title: Monday.com
item.description:
Monday.com organizes work in colorful boards that resemble spreadsheets. Teams track projects, sales pipelines, marketing campaigns, and operations with columns for status, owners, dates, and more, and view the same data as a timeline, calendar, or chart. No-code automations handle routine updates and notifications.

The platform has expanded into products for sales CRM, service desks, and software development, built on the same foundation. AI assistants create boards from a description, summarize items and updates, write content, and extract information, and agents can take on tasks within workflows.

item.title: Motion
item.description: Motion tries to take planning off your hands. You add tasks with deadlines, durations, and priorities, connect your calendar, and Motion places each task into open time on your calendar. If a meeting gets added or a task runs long, it rebuilds the schedule automatically so you always see a realistic plan for the day. The goal is to protect focus time and make sure deadlines are met without constant manual rearranging.

item.title: Smartsheet AI
item.description:
Smartsheet is built around the grid. Teams manage projects, requests, and processes in sheets that look like spreadsheets but add features such as attachments, comments, dependencies, and approvals. The same data can be viewed as a Gantt chart, calendar, board, or form, and reports and dashboards summarize progress for leaders. It’s used for project plans, marketing calendars, intake processes, and portfolio tracking in many large organizations.

Automation and AI reduce manual work. Rules can send alerts, request approvals, or update fields when conditions are met, and AI helps by generating formulas from plain language, summarizing sheets, creating content, and analyzing data to find trends. Newer features allow building workflows and agents with natural language. Integrations connect with Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Slack, Salesforce, and more.

item.title: Taskade
item.description:
Taskade merges project management and AI. A project can be viewed as a list, board, calendar, table, or mind map, and everything can be edited collaboratively in real time. Chat and video calls are built into the workspace so a team can discuss and track tasks in one place. It is flexible enough for personal to-do lists, team projects, wikis, and meeting notes.

AI agents are central. Users can create agents with specific roles and knowledge, such as a research assistant, a project manager, or a support bot, and let them generate content, break down projects, and respond to questions. Automations connect actions across tools and trigger agents on schedules or events, and templates cover common uses like content planning and sales processes. You can also generate whole projects from a prompt.

item.title: x.ai
item.description: x.ai took a distinctive approach to scheduling. Instead of an app or a booking link, you copied its assistant, Amy or Andrew, on an email thread, and it handled the back-and-forth of finding a time with the other people. It read your calendar, proposed times in natural language, replied to the guests, and sent calendar invitations. Because everything happened by email, the other person did not need to install or log in to anything.

item.title: Fantastical
item.description:
Fantastical is known for natural language entry. A user types a phrase such as lunch with Sam next Tuesday at noon, and the app creates the event with the right time, place, and attendees. It shows calendars from many accounts in one view, including Google, iCloud, and Exchange, along with tasks and reminders.

Scheduling features help with coordination. Users can share availability and let others book time, propose several slots to a group, and attach video conference details automatically. Newer AI features help with preparation for meetings and smart suggestions, and the app integrates with other tools through its calendar sets and openings.

item.title: Jira
item.description:
Jira tracks work through issues in boards, backlogs, and timelines. Software teams use it for sprints, bug tracking, and roadmaps, and many other teams use it for requests and projects. Workflows are customizable, and it integrates with code hosts, chat tools, and the rest of Atlassian’s products.

Atlassian has added AI across Jira. It summarizes long ticket discussions, drafts descriptions and subtasks, and turns natural language into search queries. Rovo agents can take on work such as triaging issues or answering questions across connected tools, and the AI draws on a team’s own data.

item.title: Team Pulse
item.description:
Team Pulse offers tasks, boards, and status views for small teams. AI helps summarize progress, flag risks, and keep everyone informed, aiming to reduce the status meetings and check-ins that eat time.

The product competes with well-known tools and aims at teams that find larger platforms heavy. Common features include assignments, deadlines, and dashboards that show workload.

Independent information is limited, so evaluate it with a trial, including integrations and export options. It has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Asana, Monday.com, ClickUp, Linear, and Trello. Team Pulse suits small teams looking for a simple tracker.
